messages.author: c31b814f354c0f4b
messages.subject: How much percent of sample size of the total area to take for Occupancy modelling in a mountain terrain
parts:
Hello!

I want to do a occupancy modelling of multiple species and for that have stratified my study area into 9 elevational bands ranging from 500m to 4500m at every 500m of interval (<500m,500 - 1000m....4000-4500m). The entire elevational bands represents the  distributional range of my species. I ran a zonal statistics in QGIS of the 9 elevational classes on 1 x 1 km grid. The output gave me 4345 grid cells (representing all 9 classes). Even if I take 2% of 4345 it will come to 87 no. of grid cells. Let's say it will take me 2 days to conduct multiple transects in each grid, which means to survey the entire 87 grids it will take me 87 x 2 = 174 days (5 months) to cover the entire grid cells for occupancy survey. I also want to see the  seasonal variations in occupancy . Hence, what percent of sample size shall I take of the total study area (4345 grids x 1 sq km) so that I could have more time to conduct replicate surveys for the seasonal occupancy without compromising on optimal sample size coverage percent.

These are my no. of grids in the 9 elevation class (in meters) from zonal statistics in Qgis.

> 500 - 14
500- 1000 - 99 grids
1000 - 1500 - 146 grids
1500 - 2000- 158 grids
2000- 2500- 136 grids
2500 -3000 - 134 grids 
3000- 3500- 127 grids
3500- 4000- 130 grids 
4000-4500 - 341 grids

messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] How much percent of sample size of the total area to take for Occupancy modelling in a mountain terrain
parts:
Dear Atharva,

your question just makes me think that there is that alternative design for an occupancy study known as "time-to-detection" (ttd). This is a continuous-time observation protocol, where you note the time (in minutes, seconds) between the start of a survey and the moment when you detect the first individual of each species (see papers by Garrard et al., Austral Ecology, 2008, Bornand et al., MEE, 2014 among others). We also have a section on ttd designs in the AHM1 book, and Ken Kellner has recently included it into unmarked (for single species only).

The greatest thing about this design is perhaps that you can estimate occupancy and detection separately from just a single visit. Hence, in your case this would mean that you could half your survey effort or double the number of sites surveyed.

You should look into this design perhaps. It is much less well-known than the standard designs and hardly ever used, although it's been 12 years now since Garrard et al first described it. I am puzzled by the rarity of its use, since it offers such obvious logistical benefits, as one visit is already enough.

If you wanted to do multispecies analyses with data collected under this design, then you could not (currently) do this in unmarked (nor in PRESENCE or MARK, as far as I know, though I may be wrong). However, it would be trivial to fit such a community occupancy model in BUGS software (or anything else if you have a very good friend who is a statistician).

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.author: 247b990d236a7af6
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] How much percent of sample size of the total area to take for Occupancy modelling in a mountain terrain
parts:
Two general comments:

(1) When sampling a large population, it is the total number of samples that typically drives everything as opposed to the percent of the area being sampled.

(2) One needs to know how good the precision needs to be to judge the adequacy of the sampling.  That is a subject matter rather than a statistical issue.  Sample size and percent of area sampled cannot tell you that.

Jim
